title: $950,000 Mortgage Payment by Rate & Term (2026)
metaDescription: A $950,000 mortgage costs $6,004.65/mo at 6.5% over 30 years ($8,275.52 on 15). See payments at 5–7.5%, total interest, and the income needed.

hero.lede: Principal-and-interest payments on a $950,000 home loan across 5.0%–7.5% rates and 15/30-year terms, plus total interest, a first-year amortization schedule, and the income the 28% rule implies.

shortAnswer.heading: What does a $950,000 mortgage cost per month?
shortAnswer.html: A $950,000 mortgage costs about $6,004.65 a month in principal and interest at 6.5% on a 30-year fixed term, or $8,275.52 on a 15-year. Depending on your rate (5.0%–7.5%), the 30-year payment runs $5,099.81–$6,642.54. Total 30-year interest at 6.5%: $1,211,674.

sections.title: $950,000 mortgage payment by rate and term.
sections.note: Principal and interest only — add property taxes, homeowners insurance, and PMI (if under 20% down) for the full monthly cost.

sections.title: What $950,000 of mortgage debt really costs.
paragraphs: Borrow $950,000 at 6.5% for 30 years and the principal-and-interest payment is $6,004.65 per month. Choose 15 years instead and you pay $8,275.52 monthly, yet total interest falls from $1,211,674 to $539,594 — the shorter term keeps $672,080 in your pocket.

A single percentage point matters enormously at this size: 6.0% versus 7.0% on a 30-year $950,000 loan is $624.64 more every month, or about $224,870 over 360 payments. That's why the payment table spans $5,099.81 (at 5.0%) to $6,642.54 (at 7.5%).

sections.title: Total interest on $950,000 over the full term.
sections.note: At 6.5% on a 30-year term you repay $2,161,674 in total — 2.28× the amount borrowed.

sections.title: First-year amortization: where each payment actually goes.
sections.note: In year one you pay $61,437 of interest but only $10,618 of principal — early payments are mostly interest, which is why extra principal payments early on save so much.

sections.title: PMI, income needed, and the rest of the bill.
paragraphs: If your down payment is under 20% of the purchase price, expect private mortgage insurance on top: typically 0.5–1% of the loan per year, or roughly $396–$792 a month on $950,000. With 20% down, a $950,000 loan corresponds to about a $1,187,500 home — and no PMI. Property taxes and homeowners insurance also come on top of every figure here.

Lenders often screen affordability with the 28% rule: housing below 28% of gross income. Covering $6,004.65 a month of P&I under that rule takes about $257,342 a year of income. Because taxes and insurance stack on top, real qualifying incomes run higher.

sections.title: Nearby loan amounts at 6.5%.
sections.note: Income column applies the 28% front-end rule to the 30-year P&I payment only; taxes and insurance push the real requirement higher.

faq.q: What is the monthly payment on a $950,000 mortgage?
faq.a: At 6.5% on a 30-year fixed, a $950,000 mortgage costs $6,004.65 a month in principal and interest. Across rates from 5.0% to 7.5%, the 30-year payment ranges from $5,099.81 to $6,642.54. Property taxes, insurance, and PMI come on top.

faq.q: How much income do I need for a $950,000 mortgage?
faq.a: Using the 28% front-end rule on the $6,004.65 payment (6.5%, 30-year), you'd want roughly $257,342 of gross annual income for the principal and interest alone. Since lenders count taxes, insurance, PMI, and your other debts too, a comfortable qualifying income is typically higher.

faq.q: How much interest will I pay on a $950,000 mortgage?
faq.a: At 6.5%, total interest comes to $1,211,674 over a 30-year term versus $539,594 over 15 years — the shorter term saves $672,080. In the first year alone the 30-year loan accrues $61,437 of interest against just $10,618 of principal reduction.

faq.q: Is a 15-year or 30-year term better for a $950,000 loan?
faq.a: The 30-year payment ($6,004.65 at 6.5%) is $2,270.87 cheaper per month than the 15-year ($8,275.52), but costs $672,080 more in lifetime interest. Choose 15 years if the payment fits comfortably; otherwise take the 30-year and make extra principal payments when you can.

faq.q: Does the $950,000 payment include taxes and insurance?
faq.a: No — every figure on this page is principal and interest only. Budget extra for property tax and homeowners insurance (often several hundred dollars monthly, varying by state), plus PMI of roughly $396–$792/month if your down payment is under 20%. With 20% down, $950,000 of financing corresponds to about a $1,187,500 purchase price.

methodology: Payments use the standard amortization formula M = P·r(1+r)ⁿ / ((1+r)ⁿ − 1) with monthly compounding, on a $950,000 principal. Rates shown (5.0%–7.5%) are illustrative steps, not quotes — your rate depends on credit, points, and the market.
The amortization table applies 6.5%/30-year, computing interest on the running balance each month and rounding to cents, the way a servicer statement does.
All figures are principal and interest only. Property tax, homeowners insurance, HOA dues, and PMI are excluded except where explicitly estimated (PMI shown at 0.5–1% of the loan per year).
Income-needed figures apply the 28% front-end ratio to P&I only. Educational estimates — not lending, tax, or financial advice.
